senses.d: Someone possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill; especially somebody who has demonstrated this by a creative or original work in science, music, art, etc.
ex: She's a genius; she won a Nobel Prize at fifteen!
Marx stand höher, sah weiter, überblickte mehr und rascher als wir andern alle. Marx war ein Genie, wir andern höchstens Talente.

senses.d: Extraordinary mental capacity.
Inspiration, a mental leap, an extraordinary creative process.
ex: a work of genius
to add a dash of cinnamon amid such umami was pure genius

senses.d: The tutelary deity or spirit of a place or person.
ex: and the genius of the place: the growing enthusiasm for codified standards in the Army and Navy

senses.d: Ingenious, brilliant, very clever, or original.
ex: What a genius idea!
But Vahul was more genius than Rishi.

grp.label: someone possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin generātus, perfect passive participle of generō (“beget, procreate, produce”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

senses.d: To bring into being; give rise to.
ex: The discussion generated an uproar.
The Ecclesiastical Commission was generated by Sir Robert Peel and bore the marks of Peel’s personality; bureaucratic, capable and cold.

senses.d: To produce as a result of a chemical or physical process.
ex: Adding concentrated sulphuric acid to water generates heat.

senses.d: To procreate, beget.
ex: They generated many offspring.

senses.d: To form a figure from a curve or solid.
ex: Rotating a circle generates a sphere.

senses.d: To appear or occur; be generated.
Generated, not self-existent.

chain.g: of the same family or clan

ety.text: From Middle English gentil (“courteous, noble”), from Old French gentil (“high-born, noble”), from Latin gentilis (“of the same family or clan”), from gens (“[Roman] clan”). Doublet of gentile, genteel, and jaunty.

senses.d: Tender and amiable; of a considerate or kindly disposition.
ex: Stuart is a gentle man; he would never hurt you.
A good heart, these days, is hard to find / So please be gentle with this heart of mine

senses.d: Soft and mild rather than hard or severe.
ex: I felt something touch my shoulder; it was gentle and a little slimy.
Here the stripped panelling was warmly gold and the pictures, mostly of the English school, were mellow and gentle in the afternoon light.

senses.d: Docile and easily managed.
ex: We had a gentle swim in the lake.
a gentle horse

senses.d: Gradual rather than steep or sudden.
ex: The walks in this area have a gentle incline.

senses.d: Polite and respectful rather than rude.
ex: He gave me a gentle reminder that we had to hurry up.

senses.d: Well-born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.
ex: "You are of gentle blood," she said […]
the studies wherein our noble and gentle youth ought to bestow their time

senses.d: To become gentle.
To ennoble.
ex: […] For he to-day that sheds his blood with me / Shall be my brother; be he ne'er so vile, / This day shall gentle his condition […]

senses.d: To break; to tame; to domesticate.
To soothe; to calm; to make gentle.
A person of high birth.
ex: Gentles, methinks you frown.
‘Gentles and fair lady, if you have suffered ill usage or hardship, I pray you lay such complaints before me[.]’

senses.d: A maggot used as bait by anglers.
ex: Pooh! the whole thing is as alive and wrigging as an angler's box of gentles

senses.d: A trained falcon, or falcon-gentil.

Latin -iusnom. Latin -ium Latin -cīdiumder. Middle French -cidebor. English -cide English genocide From the stem of Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “race, kind”) (cognate with Latin gēns (“tribe, clan”), whence genus), corresponding to geno- + -cide (“killing”). Piecewise doublet of gendercide. Compare genticide.

senses.d: The systematic and deliberate destruction of a group of people; typically by killing substantial numbers of them, on the basis of their ethnicity, religion, nationality, or similar grounds.
ex: A genocide will always be followed by the denial that it ever happened.
For the German occupying authorities war thus appears to offer the most appropriate occasion for carrying out their policy of genocide.

senses.d: The systematic suppression of ideas or practices on the basis of cultural or ethnic origin; culturicide.
ex: linguistic genocide

senses.d: The elimination of an entire class of monsters by the player in roguelikes.
To commit genocide (against); to eliminate (a group of people) completely.
ex: A clue appears in the Nazis finding the Gypsies dirty and disorderly (for not only Jews were genocided).

grp.label: systematic killing of substantial numbers of people
